Campagne de levée de fonds 2026
CathoSV
blocks.text:
Campagne de levée de fonds 2026
CathoSV

blocks.html:
​Ensemble, faisons vivre et grandir notre communauté !

​

Chers amis,

​

Le moment est venu de lancer notre campagne annuelle de levée de fonds CathoSV !

​

Cette année, notre objectif est de récolter 30 000 $ d’ici le 31 décembre 2026, afin d’assurer la pérennité de CathoSV et de maintenir la présence de prêtres francophones au sein de notre communauté.

​

10 ans d’une belle aventure humaine et spirituelle !

​

Il y a maintenant une dizaine d'années, CathoSV voyait le jour avec une ambition simple mais essentielle : permettre aux catholiques francophones de la baie de San Francisco de vivre, partager et faire grandir leur foi ensemble, en français.

​

Que de chemin parcouru depuis !

​

Aujourd’hui, nous avons la chance d’être accueillis au sein de la paroisse Saint Nicholas–Saint William et de compter sur trois prêtres francophones engagés à nos côtés : les Pères Basile, Didier et Damien.

Le Père Johannes nous fait également la joie de venir célébrer une messe en français chaque mois.

​

Au fil des années, CathoSV est devenue bien plus qu’une communauté paroissiale : une grande famille, unie, ouverte et accueillante, avec cet esprit « startup family » qui nous ressemble tant !

​

Une communauté à notre image, avec nos forces, nos talents, nos imperfections, mais surtout notre envie commune de cheminer dans la foi et de grandir ensemble.

​

Pourquoi avons-nous besoin de vous ?

Pour que cette belle aventure continue, nous avons besoin de votre soutien.

L’intégralité des fonds récoltés lors de cette campagne sera consacrée à maintenir la présence de prêtres francophones.

​

Derrière chaque messe, chaque sacrement, chaque rencontre et chaque moment de partage, il y a des prêtres qui consacrent leur temps et leur énergie à notre communauté.

Les soutenir matériellement, c’est leur permettre de poursuivre leur mission auprès de nous, de nos familles et de nos prochains. 

​

Combien donner ? Chacun selon ses possibilités !

Il n’y a pas de petit don !

Chacun est libre de contribuer selon ses moyens et son envie.

Les années précédentes, les dons ont varié de 15 $ à 3 000 $, preuve que chaque participation compte.

À titre de repère, l’Église encourage une contribution généreuse et proportionnée à ses ressources. Une fourchette de 1 à 5 % de ses revenus peut constituer un point de référence, à adapter à sa situation personnelle.
Vos dons peuvent également être déductibles des impôts. 

​

Le corporate matching : un formidable moyen de multiplier votre générosité !

​

Saviez-vous que de nombreuses entreprises américaines proposent de doubler, voire de tripler, les dons de leurs salariés à des associations éligibles ?

C’est le principe du corporate matching.

L’année dernière, ce dispositif a représenté un tiers du montant total de notre collecte !

Alors, avant de faire votre don, pensez à vérifier si votre employeur propose ce programme. Un simple geste peut considérablement augmenter l’impact de votre générosité, sans dépense supplémentaire de votre part.

​

Ensemble, construisons l’avenir de CathoSV !

Depuis dix ans, CathoSV grandit grâce à l’engagement, à l’énergie et à la générosité de chacun d’entre vous.

Aujourd’hui, nous faisons appel à cette même générosité pour poursuivre notre mission et permettre aux générations présentes et futures de continuer à vivre leur foi en français au cœur de la Silicon Valley.

​

Chaque don compte. Chaque geste nous rapproche de notre objectif.

​

Merci du fond du cœur pour votre confiance, votre fidélité et votre soutien.

Ensemble, continuons à faire vivre et grandir CathoSV !

​

L’équipe CathoSV

​

> Fonctionnement du corporate matching

blocks.html:
Il est toujours temps de faire le premier (ou deuxième) pas pour devenir chrétien !

Vous n'avez pas été baptisé.e, pas encore reçu votre première communion ou votre confirmation ?

 

À partir de janvier 2027, CathoSV propose un parcours vers les sacrements en français pour les adultes, à San Francisco et dans la Bay Area.

Grâce à un accompagnement personnalisé, vous pourrez apprendre à connaître Dieu et à vivre l'Évangile, à votre rythme, au sein d'une communauté chaleureuse.

blocks.html:
Novembre, un mois pour prier pour nos défunts

​

Et si, en ce mois de novembre, nous prenions le temps de confier à Dieu ceux qui nous ont quittés ?

​

Dans la tradition catholique, novembre est tout particulièrement consacré à la prière pour les défunts. Après la fête de la Toussaint, le 1er novembre, où nous célébrons tous les saints, l’Église nous invite, le 2 novembre, à faire mémoire de tous les fidèles défunts.

​

Mais pourquoi et comment prier pour ceux qui sont morts ?

CathoSV vous a préparé un article sur ce sujet à retrouver sur notre blog ou sur nos réseaux sociaux.


« Et si, tout au long du mois de novembre, chacun de nous prenait l'habitude de prier chaque jour pour un défunt ? Un parent, un ami, une personne oubliée ou une âme pour laquelle personne ne prie.

Une petite prière, un grand geste d'amour. »

​​​

blocks.text: Célébrons ensemble les 60 ans de Monseigneur Cantú !

blocks.html:
Cette année, le diocèse de San Jose organise une semaine fraternelle du 30 novembre au 5 décembre 2026 à l’occasion des 60 ans de Mgr Cantu.

L’objectif est de rassembler toutes les communautés du diocèse pour prier ensemble et apprendre à mieux se connaître.


Le recueillement aura lieu toute la semaine. Voir le programme ci-dessous :​​

Hope for the unhoused
Dimanche  20 décembre
10:30 AM - Milpitas
blocks.text:
Hope for the unhoused
Dimanche  20 décembre
10:30 AM - Milpitas

blocks.html:
Comme nous l’avons fait plusieurs fois précédemment, nous vous proposons une action solidaire avec les plus défavorisés en conjonction avec “Hope for the unhoused”.

 

Celle-ci aura lieu à Milpitas le dimanche 20 décembre à partir de 10:30 et consistera à distribuer des kits d'hygiène, vêtements et snacks à des sans-abris pendant qu’une autre association mettra à leur disposition des douches.

​

Cette activité est possible à partir de 12 ans.
 

 S'inscrire tôt nous permet de nous assurer que nous avons assez de volontaires, de plus le nombre de places est limité. 

​

Il est également possible de contribuer en apportant des manteaux et chaussures en bon état (en particulier des chaussures homme 10-11) qui seront récoltés le dimanche 13 décembre après la messe.

blocks.html: Bienvenue au Père Damien ! 🙏
blocks.text: Bienvenue au Père Damien ! 🙏

blocks.html:
C’est avec une grande joie que nous accueillons officiellement le Père Damien comme chapelain de CathoSV !

​

Après quelques mois déjà passés au sein de notre communauté, à partager nos célébrations, nos rencontres et nos moments de fraternité, le Père Damien prend désormais officiellement ses fonctions de chapelain.

​

Nous sommes très heureux de pouvoir compter sur sa présence, son enthousiasme et son engagement pour accompagner notre communauté dans sa vie spirituelle et fraternelle avec les Pères Basile et Didier.

​

Cher Père Damien, merci d’avoir accepté cette belle mission auprès de nous ! Que cette nouvelle étape soit riche en rencontres, en partage et en beaux projets au service de notre communauté.

​

Bienvenue officiellement dans la grande famille CathoSV ! 💙🙏

​

Découvrez le parcours passionnant de l'Abbé Damien Verley :

blocks.html: CathoSV à l’honneur dans Aleteia !
blocks.text: CathoSV à l’honneur dans Aleteia !

blocks.html:
Nous sommes heureux et fiers de voir notre communauté CathoSV mise à l’honneur dans les colonnes d’Aleteia, qui lui consacre un article particulièrement élogieux !

​

Pour ceux qui ne le connaissent pas encore, Aleteia est un média d’information et un quotidien en ligne catholique. Il est aujourd’hui l’un des médias chrétiens les plus consultés au monde.

​

Cette belle reconnaissance met en lumière le dynamisme de notre communauté, son engagement et sa volonté de faire vivre la foi catholique francophone au cœur de la Silicon Valley.

​

Une belle occasion de faire rayonner CathoSV bien au-delà de notre communauté !

​

Découvrez l’article ici :

blocks.html: Le regard de Père Damien sur la visite du Pape Léon XIV en France
blocks.text: Le regard de Père Damien sur la visite du Pape Léon XIV en France

blocks.html:
Cette semaine, le Père Damien a pris la plume pour revenir longuement sur la visite du Pape en France.

 

Quelle joie nous avons ressentie à vivre ces moments, et quelle grâce de voir tant de ferveur autour du Saint-Père !

Son article est à lire tranquillement, peut-être une tisane à la main :

on l'a lu d'une traite, sans pouvoir décrocher !

CathoSV, par delà la messe qui est le sommet de la vie chrétienne, nous invite à nourrir notre identité profonde de chrétien en devenant  « le sel de la terre ».
Dans cette dynamique, nous souhaitons donc continuer à embellir nos messes ainsi qu’à renforcer l’accueil, favoriser la croissance spirituelle, raviver notre esprit de mission et de service, et mettre concrètement en pratique notre raison d’être : « Le sel de la terre ».

Pour continuer notre mission,  voici la liste des postes ouverts pour la rentrée à CathoSV Los Altos :

  • Des animateurs pour la préparation des messes (avec l'aide de l'équipe liturgie)

  • Un.e responsable pour le partage d'Evangile pendant la messe

  • Un.e responsable équipe d'accueil

  • Un couple responsable Baptême des enfants de moins de 7 ans

  • Un.e responsable "Jeunes Pros"

À chacun et chacune, un immense merci !

La Prière des Mères soutient et s'adresse à toutes celles qui ont un cœur de mère et qui désirent prier ensemble pour leurs enfants, petits-enfants et tous les enfants du monde.


Nous remettons nos enfants entre les mains de Dieu. Ce que nous pouvons changer, les souffrances ou les angoisses que nous éprouvons en face de nos enfants, nous les donnons au Seigneur, croyant en sa Parole : "demandez et vous recevrez" et Il agira, à sa façon et en son temps.


Un groupe de Prière des Mères se réunit chaque jeudi matin à 9h30 à South Bay, et un soir par mois à Los Altos (la date mensuelle n'étant pas fixe se reporter au calendrier et demandez à être inscrite au groupe WhatsApp).
 

VENEZ ESSAYER !

blocks.html:
AUMÔNERIE : PORTEURS D'ESPÉRANCE
Thème du jubilé de cette année 2025
blocks.text:
AUMÔNERIE : PORTEURS D'ESPÉRANCE
Thème du jubilé de cette année 2025

blocks.html:
Retour sur notre séance d’aumônerie : Jubilé 2025, "Pèlerins d’Espérance"

 

Lors de notre dernière séance d’aumônerie High School, nous avons exploré la signification du Jubilé 2025, une année sainte célébrée par l’Église tous les 25 ans. Nous avons découvert ses origines bibliques, son institution au XIVᵉ siècle, ainsi que son sens profond : un temps de grâce, de pardon et de renouveau spirituel.

 

Cette année, le pape François a choisi de placer le Jubilé sous le signe de l’Espérance, une vertu essentielle dans un monde confronté aux crises et aux incertitudes.À travers nos échanges, et en nous appuyant sur la bulle d’indiction du pape François et sur la symbolique du logo du Jubilé, nous avons pris conscience que l’Espérance chrétienne ne se limite pas à un simple optimisme : c’est une des trois vertu théologales, celle qui oriente, indique la direction et le but de l'existence croyante.

 

L’Espérance demande un engagement, une mise en marche, c’est une attente brûlante qui invite à la conversion.

Ce message d’Espérance s’adresse avant tout aux jeunes, à un âge où l’avenir se cherche entre doutes, pressions sociales et incertitudes du monde. S’entourer de modèles inspirants, bâtir des amitiés solides et cultiver un rêve sont autant de moyens de nourrir notre Espérance. Cela nous a rappelé la citation d’Oscar Wilde : "La sagesse, c'est d'avoir des rêves suffisamment grands pour ne pas les perdre de vue lorsqu'on les poursuit”.

 

Enfin, pour mieux intégrer l’Espérance dans notre vie quotidienne, nous avons réfléchi à des actions concrètes : commencer la journée par une parole inspirante, tenir un journal de gratitude, poser chaque jour un geste d’Espérance tourné vers les autres, oser demander du soutien à nos proches, ou nous créer une « ancre d’espérance », un repère solide qui nous recentre dans les moments de doute. Cela peut être un rituel simple, comme allumer une bougie pour prier, méditer sur la fidélité de Dieu ou consacrer du temps chaque semaine à la messe.

 

À l’issue de cette rencontre, chacun est reparti avec une réflexion personnelle pour l’année à venir : comment puis-je, à mon échelle, devenir un pèlerin d’Espérance ?

CATHOSV: Hello and thank you for sharing this evening with us! Could you please start by introducing yourselves?

 

GV: Hi! I am Deacon Gerardo Vázquez, from the Archdiocese of San Francisco. I was born in Mexico, raised in Fresno California and I moved to the Bay Area in 2001. I studied aerospace engineering. I worked for NASA, Lockheed Martin and Pratt and Whitney for about 12 years. I got the call and entered the seminary at 33 years old. Actually I entered the seminary at the same time as your pastor, Fr Robain Lamba! Today I am a transitional Deacon and I will be ordained on June 4 of this year.

Fr Robain and I entered the seminary in the same year but I actually took a year off, because I wasn't sure what particular diocese I was called to. I traveled a year to Mexico because I have an uncle who was a priest down there. And then I traveled to Rome. I studied there for about six months . After traveling for a while, I realized that “thank God I'm called to the priesthood still”, but specifically in San Francisco. So I came back! 

 

BC: Hi! I am Benjamin Condon, from the diocese of Sacramento. I graduated from High School in 2006. I entered the seminary just after High School at 18 years old. That was in 2016 and I spent four years at a seminary in Oregon called Mount Angel seminary. 

It is a beautiful seminary attached to a Benedictine monastery founded in 1880. I entered the college seminary there and I graduated with a degree in philosophy. That's the prerequisite for anybody who wants to enter seminary without a college major in theology. For example Deacon Gerardo already had a degree so he entered something called pre theology, which means he just got a certificate of philosophy and then moved on to study theology.

I arrived at St Patrick seminary in 2020 and I am 3 years away from ordination! In total I will have spent 9 years at the seminary.

 

CATHOSV: That’s a lot!

 

BC:  It is a way of putting it! They really are trying to make sure you are ready.

 

GV: It's like being engaged for a very long time or dating someone for very long before you actually get married!

 

BC: There is all of the maturing that needs to happen and all of the spiritual preparation, mental preparation and all the academic studies!

 

CATHOSV: Tell us a little bit more about your studies, how many classes do you take as a seminarian?

 

BC: I have 6 classes and 7 periods. Each period is either 50mn or 75mn, it certainly keeps you busy!  Every Wednesday is off but we still have morning prayers, so very little free time! To keep up with everything takes a lot. I mean, just within this month, I'll have 30 pages worth of papers to write. 

 

AV: Some students have field education, this means they go to either a parish, or like Catholic Charities or St. Vincent De Paul or other Catholic organizations that are in the area. They spend four hours roughly. As a deacon, I don't have that, but I go to a parish and serve as a deacon and have to be at the parish for at least 24 hours per weekend. So on top of my classes that I'm doing that.

 

CATHOSV: Benjamin you entered the seminary at 18 years old, just after High School. How were you introduced to Philosophy and Theology? These subjects are not taught in High Schools in the United States?

 

BC: It is true that in the public school system in the United States, they have toned down most of the arts and philosophy with a bigger focus on STEM, science, technology, engineering, mathematics. I grew up in a special high school program called the “Great Books program”. It means that my High School studies was reading ancient Western philosophy, all the way from the Greeks, the Romans and the medieval ages. That was a private program in High School.

 

GV: When I entered seminary, as an engineer, I was quite prepared and I was able to double major and apply for honors. I was actually able to use all of my studies. It was great, I loved it. I really enjoyed the time I got to dig into a topic. When there's a topic, it's similar to how an engineer approaches a problem. I mean, you could talk about this. It's not necessarily that you have a situation and you call it a problem, and you don't know what to do with it. No, it's a situation where you have a solution and you want to see how it applies. And so I love that.

 

CATHOSV: It looks like the seminarists here have a great variety of backgrounds, interests and careers, can you tell us more about it?

 

GV: It is true that most of the seminarians had work experience before arriving here. With all different kinds of backgrounds: lawyers, engineers, state senators, nurses, doctors and even an opera singer and a colonel who worked at the Pentagon! It is great to meet so many different people. Each one brings his own expertise, for example when we have to organize an event or a retreat. And we used to organize and host many big events before the pandemic, for the celebration of Our Lady of Guadeloupe, ST Patrick, Korean martyrs, and our annual Gala.

 

BC: That's so great, it's the coolest thing. When I entered seminary I was right out of high school with very little experience … about anything really. At the seminary, I meet guys who are league lawyers who are construction workers. I met a guy who was a site engineer, he would organize the construction of these 678 storey tall buildings, these million dollar projects, and here he is in seminary and he's just like another guy, you know. And so here I am, and just hanging out with these guys in the back patio, and they’re just talking about these stories.  

 

CATHOSV: Can you talk a little bit about how all those different experiences impact the life of the community here?

 

BC: Oh, yeah, very easily. All of the guys bring their own experience. So when we have events, the seminary guys will bring their expertise in one way or another. Once a month, we would go on some outdoor excursions, we go hiking, we go skiing, snowshoeing, cross country skiing, and a big part of that is the organization.  We put on retreats for like a third of the seminary. So 50 guys come and join us on these events, and the seminarians are all in charge of organizing that. And so for me coming out of high school, I had very little experience in how to organize an event for 50 people. And these guys are stepping up using the skills that they know. For example, there's a few of the guys who studied music. One of the guys here is an opera singer, he is able to use his talents and liturgy all the time. That really adds to the beauty of what the seminary has.

 

GV: I'm actually involved with the “Institute for Advanced physics”. Archbishop Corleone asked me to get involved with the group. And now I'm an associate member. Science is my background, but combining it with theology makes it really great. Combining faith and science reality is much needed. The Archbishop also gives me permission. We just recently had a retreat with the Archdiocese and the military services, so I got permission to become a military chaplain as well. So after three years of being ordained, in the military, in the Archdiocese, I could go into the military branch, in the Navy. So it's really, really great. I have worked 12 years with the military, so I am pretty used to that environment. The fact that I'm going into that now as a future priest, that is pretty awesome.

 

CATHOSV: We could imagine that you live in a “closed world” without getting out of this place and without any link with the society around, but it doesn’t seem like it!

 

BC: It is not but it can feel like a closed world only because of how busy it can be here! We go out on a regular basis, we serve some charities and parishes. Every Wednesday I go out to help with ministries. And you, Deacon, are part of this Institute of science, it is a way also for the church to be present in the decisions that are made in the world. Sciences and ethics I can imagine. So it's not a closed world!

 

GV: There are also many events that are happening here. For example, the feast of San Lorenzo Luis, who is the patron saint of the Philippines, the Celebration of Our Lady of Guadeloupe which is huge event, the feast of St. Patrick's or the Korean martyrs and the Annual fundraising event. We welcome people from outside for all of these celebrations. Before the pandemic, we would have hundreds of people visiting. It's always a beautiful thing, the seminarian life is very open.

 

CATHOSV: What do you enjoy the most in your life as a seminarian?

 

BC: I do enjoy my studies a lot, even if it is a lot and even if it is difficult!! I also enjoy the fraternity that we are all able to build up here. There's a great camaraderie that can be built up very quickly. I've made a lot of friends with some of my outdoor activities that I enjoy. When we have a free weekend, we will drive to Tahoe, go skiing, and then drive back in time for classes. And so, the adventures that I get to have, it's a lot of fun. 

 

GV: My favorite time is Adoration, spending time in the large main Chapel. Especially when I am there alone, such a beautiful place for yourself! I also enjoy the Gym and the pool, we are spoiled here. You can get a little cuckoo but that's just kind of nature, everything's really provided here. 

 

CATHOSV: When you get out, the rupture with this fraternity on one campus, must be something. Is there an “after community”?

 

BC: Yes and No. I wouldn't say there is something so structured as a seminary program once we are ordained. But there are small groups, small prayer groups that priests will form that builds paternity amongst each other. Also, the friendships you form in seminary, oftentimes are very lifelong. And so even after you're ordained, you'll keep up with those friendships. I have been told though, that for some guys who've been ordained for a long time, they mentioned that one of the most difficult parts of recently being ordained, is the struggle to have that fraternity after such a direct stop to it all, like what you were mentioning. 

 

GV: Because we spend so much time together, it's a big shock. It will take some time for sure. I think that's probably why they ask us to spend 24 hours per week at a parish, just to get used to it.

 

BC:  I'm sure that many priests that you know, are probably alone out there. You can be very sure that they have a group that they meet with, at least once a month. For the priests who recognize the strength of that fraternity continuing past seminar, they will even meet twice or three times a month.

 

CATHOSV:  It's so important for them because a lot of people feel alone in their job. Having that fraternity can help them feel community.

 

BC: Even when I was in high school, you know, I had those friends I wanted to hang out with and it was a bummer when I couldn't hang out with them. You're having a nice time and suddenly, you're not hanging out together. And maybe it's more difficult to focus or maybe you're thinking like “Oh man, I really wish I was around that person right now. I really enjoyed that time with them”. And you can imagine that this could be very easily transitionable to a priest. 

 

GV:  As a priest, you are surrounded by a lot of people. And yet you can still feel alone. The important part of it is just being able to have those good relationships, healthy relationships, even with your parish family. It is important to make sure you're always available for them. Some people have their families around within their own diocese. I'm getting ordained for San Francisco but my family is in Fresno, that's about three hours away from here. It will be tough for me, but I'll travel back and forth. Priests generally get at least one day off, which is healthy, I think. But as you can imagine, Sundays are extremely busy. Especially during the Lent or Christmas season, so while people are out with their families, priests are really busy in the parish. And so that those are the moments where fraternity is essential.

 

CATHOSV: Would you say there is good mental health support for priests, if they want it?

 

BC: If they want it, yes. Unfortunately, I think some priests can isolate themselves. Because when you get older, there's that sense of “I'm just used to me, like this way of life and I don't want to change” and that's not very healthy. Just like you can get stuck in a marriage! The healthier way would be to make sure you do interact, you maintain your friendships, and reach out if you need any help.

 

CATHOSV: Would you say there's like a stigma around mental health of priests?

 

BC: No, I wouldn't say so. I think there is certainly the sense of independence that is needed. And if you're not able to practice a certain amount of independence it can be a problem. But when the priest needs help with one thing or another, when he's struggling with isolation or loneliness, it is pretty obvious, think of how much of a public figure he is. There's usually a lot of support available for the priest. Quite a lot. I think the older you get, and the more isolated you become, that's when it gets worse.

 

GV: There has been a survey “in which careers are people the happiest”? Priests are actually number one, surprisingly. Because they're doing what they're called to do. So it's not absolutely perfect, you know, like anything, like even in marriage, right? 

 

CATHOSV: It is certainly mission driven by a mission that you firmly believe in, so that makes you happy. I mean, that works in business as well as in life!

 

GV: When you're doing something that is more than just a job, that's your entire being, it's your life, and you live that out completely, with joy. That's when you feel more fulfilled. There are some that may get tired. For example, if there are not enough priests, there can be somewhat of a burnout. That’s why we need to pray for vocations. That's why we prayed the Rosary today at Vespers. From 1964 to 2004, which is 40 years, 70,000 priests left the priesthood, but the number of Catholics have actually doubled. 

 

CATHOSV: What are the most difficult aspects of your life as a seminarian, your main struggles?

 

BC: The biggest struggle for me is to combine all the dimensions of our seminarian life: the academic dimension (studies), the spiritual dimension (how you are growing in your relationship to Christ), our prayer life (intercession), our pastoral mission (ability to minister) and our human formation (how we grow in virtue). Integrating all these dimensions, that is the plan. It is a struggle to do all that together. When you have a lot of papers to write then you have less time Keep everything in a balance is the difficult part.

 

GV: Being a Deacon, I have been through most of all that, so this integration is easier for me. I always focus on God. For example, I am used to pray before and after my studies, it has become a habit. In my interactions with people, I used to overanalyze a lot, I am an engineer, a very analytical person! Because I am aware of that, I know that I have to listen more to the voice of Christ, asking myself how can I really help this person, understanding the human person in a deeper way, instead of over analyzing. It is difficult for me but it has become beautiful. 

 

CATHOSV: Many managers go through leadership programs in their companies. As future priests, are you having any training in leadership or management? A priest has the absolute leadership role! 

 

BC: No, not explicitly. We are trained on how to lead the ministries of the sacraments or how to lead a confession for example. But when it comes to managing a community, a budget, I think we do not have enough management training. Seminarians should constantly observe and ask questions to people who are doing these jobs, comparing and learning on the job! As soon as you are ordained, I heard that many problems will arrive! And you wish you would have a little more practice ;-)

 

GV: It is true that a pastor is like a mini CEO, with many people to take care of, and a doctor of many souls! Having worked in the industry for 12 years, it is very helpful to have benefited from these leadership and finances experiences. I think it is easier for pastors who had work experience prior to seminary. But leadership can certainly be learned and I definitely wish for more leadership training here. A way of progressing is also to get involved in projects here at the seminary, such as big event organizations. You learn a lot when you take these roles.

 

CATHOSV: Having said that, isn’t Jesus Christ the best school of Leadership?

 

BC: Yes, implicitly though. Many classes and conferences we have here bend towards the idea of “what you are learning you got to be able to share”. We are practicing teaching, the ability of presenting in front of many people. What is a homelie, if not a big presentation! 

 

GV: Some bishops work on the gap between the older priests and the younger priests. They implement mentorship programs. We focus a lot on the academics during our time at the seminary because we won’t have much time to study after our ordination. And we need to be ready, especially here in California where people are very well educated and ask very deep and good questions. It is very helpful to have this mentorship for more practical questions, we can ask questions about how to deal with conflict management, different council groups, and mental illness for example. If you are open to learning you can learn a lot!

 

BC: Another challenge is to get the right people on the staff, to know how to lay off people if they do a really bad job. It is difficult to fire people, especially if they have been there for a long time. It requires a lot of experience and a lot of training. 

 

CATHOSV: What are the sacrifices that you make by choosing to become a seminarian and a priest? How do you deal with them?

 

GV: First, naturally, entering the priesthood, you sacrifice the possibility of getting married. As a transitional deacon, directed to priesthood, I chose to give my entire person to God. My entire energy, my entire person. It is not just a 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM kind of job. It is like becoming a dad or a mom, you are on 24/7. You don’t stop being a priest. My sacrifice is marriage and having children, which is something you really need to discern because if you went to priesthood because you didn’t want children, it is not necessarily a good thing. You should not run away from something.

You know, I was about to get engaged before entering the seminary. But God kept calling me, to love him in an infinite way. My fiance is today happily married (her 3 ex-fiancés entered the seminary, she is blessed!) and I can honestly say that I am the happiest I have ever been in my entire life. Of course it is a sacrifice, but there is joy, because this is how I desired to love and to be loved.

 

BC: It is not a good sign when a young man says that he doesn’t want to have children. The very fundamental aspect of a priest is being a spiritual father. This is why we call priests “Father”. The desire of being a father is very strong in the heart of every good priest. Spiritual fatherhood or Spiritual motherhood can even have more impact on a person than his biological father. 

 

GV: The other sacrifice that I would mention is time: time is not your own anymore. Like parents! We can get a call at 3:00 AM in the morning any day of the week, because someone needs the anointing of the sick. If we don’t go, this person might die without receiving the sacrament! We have to treat them as our children. As a priest, we have all these highs and lows, celebrating mass in the morning, baptism in the day and a funeral in the evening, it is quite an emotional rollercoaster! You have to be fully present to them, joyfull at a weddings, sober inside for funerals …yeah, it is going to be tough!

 

CATHOSV : So, there is also a lot of joy that you can find in that calling?

 

GV: If you are truly called to a vocation, God usually makes it pretty clear! It is the same for marriage. You can not just enter marriage just because you assume that the culture expects you to do so, or because you don’t want to be alone. Many marriages end up in a very bad way. You can be alone in marriage, as a priest, we hear a lot about that. So, ultimately you choose a vocation because you feel called by God. And then you have to discern who to get married to. It is the same with priesthood, you have to discern if it is a diocesan priest, a benedictin, a dominican, there are different ways of living this priesthood. 

 

CATHOSV: We just participated in a listening session of the Synod on Synodality, asking ourselves what were our dreams and aspirations for the Catholic Church. What do you think that the Catholic Church could do to attract more teenagers and young adults?

 

CATHOSV: It certainly brings us a lot of joy to see young people like you that probably are going to make a difference!

 

GV: I would make a reference to the Scriptures. In Exodus, Moses frees people out of Egypt to take them to the Promised Land. The plan originally was to worship God for three days as God told them to. Ultimately, worship comes from God and not men telling God how we want to worship him. That is the very important distinction between the Protestant Churches and the Catholic Church. Protestant pastors were telling me how tired they were of always having to create their own liturgy, be creative, and attract new people. They need to have a high pump level of energy all the time. They start realizing now that they can not get that creative all the time.

The Catholic Church, in her wisdom, established the Liturgy that is the same, since the very beginning, and it is universal. In a sense you can say that “it is boring and ancient” but there has actually been a rise of people desiring for that sense of stillness and quiet in the worship. I am not saying that it is bad to jump crazy up and down when you sing (praising worship in Catholic Universities are amazing for example), but in the context of a mass, it is distinct, it is how God tells us how he desires us to worship him. The mass is God giving us his instructions on how he desires to be loved. Not so much for himself but for us, for the dignity of man. We worship him in such a way that gives us the greatest amount of dignity. Of course, lectures and music can make a big difference during mass! Some parishes offer Youth or Young adults masses which are really good because priests can focus on them in their homelies.

 

BC: In the Liturgy, all the different parts are working together. As you were saying, it is important that the different parts of mass complement each other. In masses where there is such an emphasis and an overabundance of music, it takes away the other part, such as when you are trying to focus on the eucharist, centered exactly on Christ. With music taking over, your attention is being divided. Christ has to compete with all these different things.

 

BC: There is a French word that was used during Vatican II that graved into me : “ressourcement” “return to the sources”. This is how I would think of it. I’m 24, the youth group that I grew up with, has now graduated from college and here we are, trying to find out what we are doing in life. Even in High School I was having these conversations with the same people. “What am I going to do in just in a few years?” Now, a few years have come by and we are thinking that, as young adults, we are in charge of our own faith. But how to nurture that faith? What is the best way to nurture that faith? Come to the alter! But a return to the sources in a particular way, means an authentic worship of God. Christ laid down a certain way for his apostles to follow, he gave authority to those apostles, to then preach and to teach. A return to that authentic worship is a very powerful thing, especially in a world where, let’s be honest, it is kind of hard to find something authentic. Look at Politics around us! Even the understanding of the human person is being stripped away, it becomes difficult to say what a human person is in the eyes of the world. But in a consistent Church, that is trying to find authenticity in a world where there is a lack of authenticity, . My experience with the hundreds of young adults i hang out with and go on hikes and retreats together, we are finding a great, great source in this authentic worship of the Church.

 

CATHOSV : We are also consistently being stimulated by phones, we are always busy, even when we have nothing to do… There is this culture of non-stop activity. I think “returning to the sources” is also taking a minute out of everything and focus on your faith. I think it is very important to share this perspective.

 

BC: Here we are hanging out together. You are all in High School. The busy-ness of High School is real, there is a lot: classes, sports, maybe a job in the evening, hanging out with friends, you are non-stop! And the rest… the moment of rest and silence, especially when I am in Adoration, the whole world stops and I can just focus on someone who matters more than anything else, and then, that being expressed in the Liturgy…it is so powerful.

 

GV: It reminds me of a Scripture that says “Be still and know I am God”! Ultimately that is what the heart and mind want, this rest. It is important to integrate that to your life, focus on what’s good, what’s true and what’s beautiful. Those things can point you to God. The modern culture has lost that, all that noise and distraction can drift you away.

 

CATHOSV : Thank you very much for your precious time, for your sincerity and openness. This conversation will resonate with us for a long time and we can’t wait to share it with the French Catholic Community. We hope to welcome you at a French Mass in Los Altos very soon!

 

Interview by Aimée, Faustine, Hector and Maelys @St Patrick’s Seminary, California, April 2022.

CATHOSV: Can you talk a little bit about how all those different experiences impact the life of the community here?
 
BC: Oh, yeah, very easily. All of the guys bring their own experience. So when we have events, the seminary guys will bring their expertise in one way or another. Once a month, we would go on some outdoor excursions, we go hiking, we go skiing, snowshoeing, cross country skiing, and a big part of that is the organization.  We put on retreats for like a third of the seminary. So 50 guys come and join us on these events, and the seminarians are all in charge of organizing that. And so for me coming out of high school, I had very little experience in how to organize an event for 50 people. And these guys are stepping up using the skills that they know. For example, there's a few of the guys who studied music. One of the guys here is an opera singer, he is able to use his talents and liturgy all the time. That really adds to the beauty of what the seminary has.
 
GV: I'm actually involved with the “Institute for Advanced physics”. Archbishop Corleone asked me to get involved with the group. And now I'm an associate member. Science is my background, but combining it with theology makes it really great. Combining faith and science reality is much needed. The Archbishop also gives me permission. We just recently had a retreat with the Archdiocese and the military services, so I got permission to become a military chaplain as well. So after three years of being ordained, in the military, in the Archdiocese, I could go into the military branch, in the Navy. So it's really, really great. I have worked 12 years with the military, so I am pretty used to that environment. The fact that I'm going into that now as a future priest, that is pretty awesome.
 
CATHOSV: We could imagine that you live in a “closed world” without getting out of this place and without any link with the society around, but it doesn’t seem like it!
 
BC: It is not but it can feel like a closed world only because of how busy it can be here! We go out on a regular basis, we serve some charities and parishes. Every Wednesday I go out to help with ministries. And you, Deacon, are part of this Institute of science, it is a way also for the church to be present in the decisions that are made in the world. Sciences and ethics I can imagine. So it's not a closed world!
 
GV: There are also many events that are happening here. For example, the feast of San Lorenzo Luis, who is the patron saint of the Philippines, the Celebration of Our Lady of Guadeloupe which is huge event, the feast of St. Patrick's or the Korean martyrs and the Annual fundraising event. We welcome people from outside for all of these celebrations. Before the pandemic, we would have hundreds of people visiting. It's always a beautiful thing, the seminarian life is very open.
 
CATHOSV: What do you enjoy the most in your life as a seminarian?
 
BC: I do enjoy my studies a lot, even if it is a lot and even if it is difficult!! I also enjoy the fraternity that we are all able to build up here. There's a great camaraderie that can be built up very quickly. I've made a lot of friends with some of my outdoor activities that I enjoy. When we have a free weekend, we will drive to Tahoe, go skiing, and then drive back in time for classes. And so, the adventures that I get to have, it's a lot of fun. 
 
GV: My favorite time is Adoration, spending time in the large main Chapel. Especially when I am there alone, such a beautiful place for yourself! I also enjoy the Gym and the pool, we are spoiled here. You can get a little cuckoo but that's just kind of nature, everything's really provided here. 
 
CATHOSV: When you get out, the rupture with this fraternity on one campus, must be something. Is there an “after community”?
 
BC: Yes and No. I wouldn't say there is something so structured as a seminary program once we are ordained. But there are small groups, small prayer groups that priests will form that builds paternity amongst each other. Also, the friendships you form in seminary, oftentimes are very lifelong. And so even after you're ordained, you'll keep up with those friendships. I have been told though, that for some guys who've been ordained for a long time, they mentioned that one of the most difficult parts of recently being ordained, is the struggle to have that fraternity after such a direct stop to it all, like what you were mentioning. 
 
GV: Because we spend so much time together, it's a big shock. It will take some time for sure. I think that's probably why they ask us to spend 24 hours per week at a parish, just to get used to it.
 
BC:  I'm sure that many priests that you know, are probably alone out there. You can be very sure that they have a group that they meet with, at least once a month. For the priests who recognize the strength of that fraternity continuing past seminar, they will even meet twice or three times a month.
 
CATHOSV:  It's so important for them because a lot of people feel alone in their job. Having that fraternity can help them feel community.
 
BC: Even when I was in high school, you know, I had those friends I wanted to hang out with and it was a bummer when I couldn't hang out with them. You're having a nice time and suddenly, you're not hanging out together. And maybe it's more difficult to focus or maybe you're thinking like “Oh man, I really wish I was around that person right now. I really enjoyed that time with them”. And you can imagine that this could be very easily transitionable to a priest. 
 
GV:  As a priest, you are surrounded by a lot of people. And yet you can still feel alone. The important part of it is just being able to have those good relationships, healthy relationships, even with your parish family. It is important to make sure you're always available for them. Some people have their families around within their own diocese. I'm getting ordained for San Francisco but my family is in Fresno, that's about three hours away from here. It will be tough for me, but I'll travel back and forth. Priests generally get at least one day off, which is healthy, I think. But as you can imagine, Sundays are extremely busy. Especially during the Lent or Christmas season, so while people are out with their families, priests are really busy in the parish. And so that those are the moments where fraternity is essential.
 
CATHOSV: Would you say there is good mental health support for priests, if they want it?
 
BC: If they want it, yes. Unfortunately, I think some priests can isolate themselves. Because when you get older, there's that sense of “I'm just used to me, like this way of life and I don't want to change” and that's not very healthy. Just like you can get stuck in a marriage! The healthier way would be to make sure you do interact, you maintain your friendships, and reach out if you need any help.
 
CATHOSV: Would you say there's like a stigma around mental health of priests?
 
BC: No, I wouldn't say so. I think there is certainly the sense of independence that is needed. And if you're not able to practice a certain amount of independence it can be a problem. But when the priest needs help with one thing or another, when he's struggling with isolation or loneliness, it is pretty obvious, think of how much of a public figure he is. There's usually a lot of support available for the priest. Quite a lot. I think the older you get, and the more isolated you become, that's when it gets worse.
 
GV: There has been a survey “in which careers are people the happiest”? Priests are actually number one, surprisingly. Because they're doing what they're called to do. So it's not absolutely perfect, you know, like anything, like even in marriage, right? 
 
CATHOSV: It is certainly mission driven by a mission that you firmly believe in, so that makes you happy. I mean, that works in business as well as in life!
 
GV: When you're doing something that is more than just a job, that's your entire being, it's your life, and you live that out completely, with joy. That's when you feel more fulfilled. There are some that may get tired. For example, if there are not enough priests, there can be somewhat of a burnout. That’s why we need to pray for vocations. That's why we prayed the Rosary today at Vespers. From 1964 to 2004, which is 40 years, 70,000 priests left the priesthood, but the number of Catholics have actually doubled. 
 
CATHOSV: What are the most difficult aspects of your life as a seminarian, your main struggles?
 
BC: The biggest struggle for me is to combine all the dimensions of our seminarian life: the academic dimension (studies), the spiritual dimension (how you are growing in your relationship to Christ), our prayer life (intercession), our pastoral mission (ability to minister) and our human formation (how we grow in virtue). Integrating all these dimensions, that is the plan. It is a struggle to do all that together. When you have a lot of papers to write then you have less time Keep everything in a balance is the difficult part.
 
GV: Being a Deacon, I have been through most of all that, so this integration is easier for me. I always focus on God. For example, I am used to pray before and after my studies, it has become a habit. In my interactions with people, I used to overanalyze a lot, I am an engineer, a very analytical person! Because I am aware of that, I know that I have to listen more to the voice of Christ, asking myself how can I really help this person, understanding the human person in a deeper way, instead of over analyzing. It is difficult for me but it has become beautiful. 
 
CATHOSV: Many managers go through leadership programs in their companies. As future priests, are you having any training in leadership or management? A priest has the absolute leadership role! 
 
BC: No, not explicitly. We are trained on how to lead the ministries of the sacraments or how to lead a confession for example. But when it comes to managing a community, a budget, I think we do not have enough management training. Seminarians should constantly observe and ask questions to people who are doing these jobs, comparing and learning on the job! As soon as you are ordained, I heard that many problems will arrive! And you wish you would have a little more practice ;-)
 
GV: It is true that a pastor is like a mini CEO, with many people to take care of, and a doctor of many souls! Having worked in the industry for 12 years, it is very helpful to have benefited from these leadership and finances experiences. I think it is easier for pastors who had work experience prior to seminary. But leadership can certainly be learned and I definitely wish for more leadership training here. A way of progressing is also to get involved in projects here at the seminary, such as big event organizations. You learn a lot when you take these roles.
 
CATHOSV: Having said that, isn’t Jesus Christ the best school of Leadership?
 
BC: Yes, implicitly though. Many classes and conferences we have here bend towards the idea of “what you are learning you got to be able to share”. We are practicing teaching, the ability of presenting in front of many people. What is a homelie, if not a big presentation! 
 
GV: Some bishops work on the gap between the older priests and the younger priests. They implement mentorship programs. We focus a lot on the academics during our time at the seminary because we won’t have much time to study after our ordination. And we need to be ready, especially here in California where people are very well educated and ask very deep and good questions. It is very helpful to have this mentorship for more practical questions, we can ask questions about how to deal with conflict management, different council groups, and mental illness for example. If you are open to learning you can learn a lot!
 
BC: Another challenge is to get the right people on the staff, to know how to lay off people if they do a really bad job. It is difficult to fire people, especially if they have been there for a long time. It requires a lot of experience and a lot of training. 
 
CATHOSV: What are the sacrifices that you make by choosing to become a seminarian and a priest? How do you deal with them?
 
GV: First, naturally, entering the priesthood, you sacrifice the possibility of getting married. As a transitional deacon, directed to priesthood, I chose to give my entire person to God. My entire energy, my entire person. It is not just a 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM kind of job. It is like becoming a dad or a mom, you are on 24/7. You don’t stop being a priest. My sacrifice is marriage and having children, which is something you really need to discern because if you went to priesthood because you didn’t want children, it is not necessarily a good thing. You should not run away from something.
You know, I was about to get engaged before entering the seminary. But God kept calling me, to love him in an infinite way. My fiance is today happily married (her 3 ex-fiancés entered the seminary, she is blessed!) and I can honestly say that I am the happiest I have ever been in my entire life. Of course it is a sacrifice, but there is joy, because this is how I desired to love and to be loved.
 
BC: It is not a good sign when a young man says that he doesn’t want to have children. The very fundamental aspect of a priest is being a spiritual father. This is why we call priests “Father”. The desire of being a father is very strong in the heart of every good priest. Spiritual fatherhood or Spiritual motherhood can even have more impact on a person than his biological father. 
 
GV: The other sacrifice that I would mention is time: time is not your own anymore. Like parents! We can get a call at 3:00 AM in the morning any day of the week, because someone needs the anointing of the sick. If we don’t go, this person might die without receiving the sacrament! We have to treat them as our children. As a priest, we have all these highs and lows, celebrating mass in the morning, baptism in the day and a funeral in the evening, it is quite an emotional rollercoaster! You have to be fully present to them, joyfull at a weddings, sober inside for funerals …yeah, it is going to be tough!
 
CATHOSV : So, there is also a lot of joy that you can find in that calling?
 
GV: If you are truly called to a vocation, God usually makes it pretty clear! It is the same for marriage. You can not just enter marriage just because you assume that the culture expects you to do so, or because you don’t want to be alone. Many marriages end up in a very bad way. You can be alone in marriage, as a priest, we hear a lot about that. So, ultimately you choose a vocation because you feel called by God. And then you have to discern who to get married to. It is the same with priesthood, you have to discern if it is a diocesan priest, a benedictin, a dominican, there are different ways of living this priesthood. 
 
CATHOSV: We just participated in a listening session of the Synod on Synodality, asking ourselves what were our dreams and aspirations for the Catholic Church. What do you think that the Catholic Church could do to attract more teenagers and young adults?
 
CATHOSV: It certainly brings us a lot of joy to see young people like you that probably are going to make a difference!
 
GV: I would make a reference to the Scriptures. In Exodus, Moses frees people out of Egypt to take them to the Promised Land. The plan originally was to worship God for three days as God told them to. Ultimately, worship comes from God and not men telling God how we want to worship him. That is the very important distinction between the Protestant Churches and the Catholic Church. Protestant pastors were telling me how tired they were of always having to create their own liturgy, be creative, and attract new people. They need to have a high pump level of energy all the time. They start realizing now that they can not get that creative all the time.
The Catholic Church, in her wisdom, established the Liturgy that is the same, since the very beginning, and it is universal. In a sense you can say that “it is boring and ancient” but there has actually been a rise of people desiring for that sense of stillness and quiet in the worship. I am not saying that it is bad to jump crazy up and down when you sing (praising worship in Catholic Universities are amazing for example), but in the context of a mass, it is distinct, it is how God tells us how he desires us to worship him. The mass is God giving us his instructions on how he desires to be loved. Not so much for himself but for us, for the dignity of man. We worship him in such a way that gives us the greatest amount of dignity. Of course, lectures and music can make a big difference during mass! Some parishes offer Youth or Young adults masses which are really good because priests can focus on them in their homelies.
 
BC: In the Liturgy, all the different parts are working together. As you were saying, it is important that the different parts of mass complement each other. In masses where there is such an emphasis and an overabundance of music, it takes away the other part, such as when you are trying to focus on the eucharist, centered exactly on Christ. With music taking over, your attention is being divided. Christ has to compete with all these different things.
 
BC: There is a French word that was used during Vatican II that graved into me : “ressourcement” “return to the sources”. This is how I would think of it. I’m 24, the youth group that I grew up with, has now graduated from college and here we are, trying to find out what we are doing in life. Even in High School I was having these conversations with the same people. “What am I going to do in just in a few years?” Now, a few years have come by and we are thinking that, as young adults, we are in charge of our own faith. But how to nurture that faith? What is the best way to nurture that faith? Come to the alter! But a return to the sources in a particular way, means an authentic worship of God. Christ laid down a certain way for his apostles to follow, he gave authority to those apostles, to then preach and to teach. A return to that authentic worship is a very powerful thing, especially in a world where, let’s be honest, it is kind of hard to find something authentic. Look at Politics around us! Even the understanding of the human person is being stripped away, it becomes difficult to say what a human person is in the eyes of the world. But in a consistent Church, that is trying to find authenticity in a world where there is a lack of authenticity, . My experience with the hundreds of young adults i hang out with and go on hikes and retreats together, we are finding a great, great source in this authentic worship of the Church.
 
CATHOSV : We are also consistently being stimulated by phones, we are always busy, even when we have nothing to do… There is this culture of non-stop activity. I think “returning to the sources” is also taking a minute out of everything and focus on your faith. I think it is very important to share this perspective.
 
BC: Here we are hanging out together. You are all in High School. The busy-ness of High School is real, there is a lot: classes, sports, maybe a job in the evening, hanging out with friends, you are non-stop! And the rest… the moment of rest and silence, especially when I am in Adoration, the whole world stops and I can just focus on someone who matters more than anything else, and then, that being expressed in the Liturgy…it is so powerful.
 
GV: It reminds me of a Scripture that says “Be still and know I am God”! Ultimately that is what the heart and mind want, this rest. It is important to integrate that to your life, focus on what’s good, what’s true and what’s beautiful. Those things can point you to God. The modern culture has lost that, all that noise and distraction can drift you away.
 
CATHOSV : Thank you very much for your precious time, for your sincerity and openness. This conversation will resonate with us for a long time and we can’t wait to share it with the French Catholic Community. We hope to welcome you at a French Mass in Los Altos very soon!
 
Interview by Aimée, Faustine, Hector and Maelys @St Patrick’s Seminary, California, April 2022.

blocks.html:
​​

L'aumônerie CathoSV propose aux ados francophones de 12 à 18 ans de:

 

  • les faire avancer sur leur chemin spirituel

  • les ouvrir à la communauté des chrétiens et les aider à y trouver leur place,

  • les aider à témoigner avec la force de l’Esprit dans l’Eglise et dans le monde.

​

Une session mensuelle: dîner partagé dans la bonne humeur, suivi d'un temps d'échanges, de réflexion et de louange.

​​

Une rencontre par mois

de 5:00 pm à 7:30 pm :

​

  • messe à 5:00 pm @ St Nicholas church, Los Altos

  • suivie de la séance d'aumônerie de 6:15 à 7:30 pm @St Nicholas parish hall 

​

​​

​​"Vous voulez sortir de votre quotidien pour discuter de sujets qui vous tiennent à coeur et découvrir comment un regard chrétien peut vous aider à vous construire dans la joie et la confiance ? Nous vous donnons rendez-vous un soir par mois pour partager un dîner ensemble".​

blocks.html:
Baptême 

 

Vous souhaitez présenter votre enfant à l'Eglise pour qu'il soit baptisé et lui ouvrir le chemin de la foi chrétienne?

Que votre enfant reçoive le baptême dans la Silicon Valley ou en France, une équipe CathoSV vous propose un parcours de préparation en français permettant la délivrance d'un certificat.

​​

Pour les enfants de 0 à 7 ans.​

  • 0-3 ans : Une réunion avec les parents 

  • 3-7 ans : Une réunion avec les parents + 1 à 2 sessions d'éveil à la foi pour les enfants futurs baptisés

​

Les parrains et marraines sont bien entendu des participants importants de la préparation, en personne ou à distance.

​

​

​​Pour les enfants de 7 à 12 ans

Un parcours sur-mesure est défini par le prêtre célébrant.

​

Vous venez d’arriver dans la Baie de San Francisco, ou vous êtes ici depuis plusieurs années et vous souhaitez rejoindre les Catholiques Francophones de la Silicon Valley, afin de  :

​

  • Connaître le lieu et l'horaire de la prochaine messe en français, les activités de catéchèse, les parcours de préparation aux sacrements, ou participer aux activités de la communauté,

  • Rencontrer un prêtre francophone, d’autres jeunes, d’autres familles catholiques de divers horizons,

  • Avancer sur votre chemin de foi, seul, en couple ou en famille.

​

Rejoignez la communauté CathoSV!​​​

​

La communauté est principalement animée par des volontaires bénévoles, et accompagnée par des prêtres francophones qui habitent la région.

​

Vous souhaitez proposer votre aide pour l'année, soumettre une idée, poser une question, envoyez-nous un message à cathosv@gmail.com

blocks.html:
​​

CathoSV propose plusieurs parcours de catéchisme en français par tranche d'âge afin de :

 

  • Permettre aux enfants de rencontrer Jésus et de découvrir que Dieu aime chacun d’entre nous,

  • Partager avec les enfants la richesse de la tradition chrétienne

  • Donner aux enfants l’occasion de réfléchir sur les questions qu’ils se posent sur eux-mêmes, le monde et Dieu.

​​

L'équipe des catéchistes s'appuie sur les manuels de l'Emmanuel pour leur sérieux, la qualité du contenu proposé, la diversité des supports ainsi que l'aide qu'ils apportent aux catéchistes dans la préparation des séances.

​

Chaque groupe est animé par un binôme de catéchistes.

​

​

  • Un dimanche par mois de 3pm à 4:30pm @ St William Church, Parish Hall, 611 S El Monte Ave, Los Altos CA

  • suivi de la messe à St Nicholas church à 5:00pm

​​​

Jeunes Pros

​

Le groupe est destiné aux jeunes chrétiens en vie active, de 25 à 35 ans.

 

Nous nous retrouvons :

  • tous les 3ème jeudi du mois à 19H30 à Nativity Church (Menlo Park) pour une soirée Adoration & Libation (libation = boisson de son choix dans le bar d'à côté en bonne compagnie) afin de réfléchir à notre responsabilité de chrétiens en entreprise et dans la société, et passer un moment convivial ! 

  • un dimanche par trimestre à SF pour une messe à Notre Dame des Victoires suivie d'un déjeuner partagé et d'un topo. 

​

​​​

Si vous êtes intéressés mais freinés pour des raisons logistiques (pas de voiture par exemple), contactez nous, il y a toujours une solution !

​

blocks.html:
Comment utiliser le Corporate Matching pour faire un don à CathoSV?

 

Rappel: La Communauté Catholique Francophone de la Silicon Valley (CathoSV) a la statut de "Parish based group" c’est à dire qu’elle bénéficie indirectement du statut d’association (statut US: 501(c)3 non-profit) de la paroisse à laquelle est elle rattachée : St. Nicholas & St. William Parish à Los Altos.

 

Plusieurs entreprises de la Silicon Valley offrent la possibilité de doubler voire tripler vos dons aux associations de votre choix si celles-ci sont répertoriées sur la plateforme Benevity (voir liste ci-dessous).

 

Depuis décembre 2020, la paroisse St. Nicholas & St. William, et donc CathoSV, est répertoriée sur Benevity, vos dons CathoSV sont donc éligibles au corporate matching une véritable opportunité pour démultiplier votre impact!

 

Voici la démarche à suivre, c'est très facile:

 

  1. Faire votre don initial sur le site internet www.cathosv.org dans la section "je donne",
    noter votre montant et la date de votre don

  2. Aller sur la plateforme Benevity via le portail de votre entreprise (ex: google.benevity.org chez Google),
    sur la page "My Dashboard"

  3. Cliquer sur "Request a match"

  4. Dans la barre de recherche “Find an eligible cause”, saisir: 
    ST. NICHOLAS & ST. WILLIAM PARISH
    Valider

  5. Dans "donation type",
    choisir "money"

  6. Saisir le montant de votre don initial + la date de votre don initial

  7. ⚠️ TRÈS IMPORTANT: dans l’espace libre "Comments",
    préciser qu’il s’agit d’un don pour la Communauté Francophone :
    "GIFT FOR THE FRENCH SPEAKING COMMUNITY"

  8. Valider "Confirm Match"


 

​

blocks.html:
Combien donner?

En France, l'Eglise recommande à ses fidèles de donner 1% de leur salaire pour le denier du culte.

Bien évidemment, chacun participe à hauteur de ce qu'il souhaite.

Tous les dons à CathoSV sont tax-deductibles.

​

L'objectif fixé avec la paroisse St Nicholas qui nous accueille est de collecter $30,000 par an. Chaque don compte!

 

Comment donner?

C'est très simple: vous pouvez faire un don tout de suite sur le site de la paroisse St Nicholas & St William

​

​

​

​

​

​

​

​

​

Comment activer le Corporate Matching?

La paroisse "St Nicholas & St William Parish" est sur la plateforme Benevity, ce qui permet de donner à CathoSV par son intermédiaire. Renseignez-vous auprès de votre employeur pour savoir s'il utilise cette plateforme. Tous les "grands" employeurs de la baie (Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon, etc) proposent un partenariat avec Benevity et ça marche!

Pour plus de détails sur comment procéder, cliquez ici.

​

​

Est-ce que je peux faire un don récurrent?

​Beaucoup plus facile pour donner sur la durée, le site vous permet de mettre en place un don récurrent. Cliquez simplement sur l'onglet "Recurring":

​

​

​

​

​

 

 

 

 

 

 

Vous pourrez créer un compte depuis lequel vous pourrez gérer vos dons. Vous pouvez annuler ou changer votre don à tous moment.

Bien entendu vous recevrez votre reçu fiscal en fin d'année avec la somme de tous vos dons.

​

Où va l'argent?

Le poste principal est celui de l'assurance maladie du Père Johannes. Les autres postes sont les différentes activités de la communauté.  Plus de détails sur les finances de CathoSV sur le blog.

​

Quel est le Tax ID de CathoSV, comment faire un don par Donor Advised Fund?

​

Pour plus de détails cliquez ici.

​

D'autres questions?

​

Pour toutes questions, contactez tresorie@cathosv.org ou fundraise@cathosv.org

​

​

blocks.html:
​

Une Equipe Notre-Dame (END) est une équipe de couples qui se soutiennent mutuellement dans leur cheminement de vie, pour vivre au quotidien leur sacrement de mariage et porter du fruit.

 

D'où viennent les END?

Le mouvement des Equipes Notre-Dame a été fondé en France par le Père Caffarel en 1947. Les END rassemblent 55 000 couples mariés repartis dans le monde. La communauté CathoSV a actuellement 3 équipes dans la baie.

 

C'est pour qui ?

Les END sont ouvertes à tout couple marié qui désire cheminer avec le Christ, personnellement et en couple, avec le soutien d'une équipe et en s'appuyant sur la pédagogie proposée par le mouvement des END.

 

Comment ça se passe ?

Les couples de chaque équipe (4 à 6 couples) accompagnés d'un prêtre, se réunissent une fois par mois autour d'un dîner. Cette réunion est l'occasion de prier ensemble, d'échanger sur un thème choisi en début d'année et de s'épauler dans notre cheminement spirituel de couple.

Toutes les équipes se réunissent aussi une fois par an, le temps d'un week-end, pour une retraite.

 

Ça se passe où ?

Les réunions se passent chaque mois chez un couple différent, membre de l'équipe.

 

Comment rejoindre la mouvement dans la région?

Si vous souhaitez constituer une équipe (4 à 6 couples maximum) ou si vous souhaitez rejoindre une équipe, contactez-nous !

​

 

Pour en savoir plus:

http://www.equipes-notre-dame.fr/

​

blocks.html: Partage d'évangile pour les 3-7 ans
blocks.text: Partage d'évangile pour les 3-7 ans

blocks.html:
Quelques dimanches durant, des sessions dédiées aux 3-7 ans les initient à l’Évangile du jour en leur proposant une lecture pédagogique et des pistes de réflexion assorties d’un atelier artistique.

 

Elles se tiennent, de la première lecture à l’homélie, en parallèle de la messe, dans le foyer adjacent à Saint Nicholas.  

​

La loi Californienne nous impose d'avoir toujours 2 adultes avec les enfants.

Afin de poursuivre cette belle aventure dans les meilleures conditions, le lien suivant vous permet de vous inscrire pour accompagner Damien et les enfants durant les prochaines dates. La seule condition est d’avoir fait  le fingerprinting et la formation correspondante. Votre seule présence lors du partage aidera déjà beaucoup !

blocks.html:
La Communauté Catholique Camerounaise de Pittsburg a été créée il y a bientôt deux ans pour rassembler les Camerounais catholiques vivant à Pittsburg et environs.  

 

L’objectif est de vivre notre Foi ensemble, dans un esprit de fraternité, d’amour et de solidarité.

 

Nous accueillons tous les frères et sœurs africains, et tous ceux qui partagent la Foi Catholique.

 

Peu importe ton origine, si tu as envie de prier, de partager et de grandir dans la foi avec d’autres, tu es le bienvenu parmi nous.
blocks.text:

Peu importe ton origine, si tu as envie de prier, de partager et de grandir dans la foi avec d’autres, tu es le bienvenu parmi nous.

blocks.html:
Nous nous réunissons chaque premier dimanche du mois à 16h30 à la paroisse Good Shepherd de Pittsburg.

C’est un moment pour prier ensemble, célébrer la messe, échanger, et partager un repas.

 

En plus de ces rencontres, nous organisons aussi une prière communautaire en ligne tous les jeudis à 20h. Cela nous permet de rester connectés dans la prière, même à distance.

 

Tout au long de l’année, nous proposons différentes activités spirituelles et éducatives, comme :

    •    Des retraites spirituelles, pour prendre du temps avec Dieu ;

    •    Des causeries et échanges avec des prêtres ou hommes de Dieu, sur des sujets de la vie quotidienne, de la famille, ou de la foi.

- L’assistance aux nécessiteux.

 

Notre but est de construire une communauté unie, où chacun se sent soutenu, écouté et encouragé.

 

Nous serions très heureux de t’accueillir parmi nous ! N’hésite pas à venir à l’une de nos rencontres ou à nous contacter pour en savoir plus.

 

Pour la Communauté 

Patrick Siewe

blocks.html:
Une vingtaine de femmes de notre communauté ont eu la grâce de vivre un pèlerinage à la suite de la vierge Marie.

Du Fiat de l’Annonciation au Magnificat de la Visitation, elles ont médité sur le Oui de Marie.

La présence de Soeur Marie, religieuse de la communauté St Jean de Colombus, Ohio, et de père Damien, leur ont permis d’alterner entre topo contemplatifs, propices à la réflexion, et briefs concrets sur la prière, les sacrements, et autres questions de vie de foi.

Au gré de la marche dans une nature splendide, chacune a pu glorifier le seigneur de tout son corps , son cœur et son âme. Certaines ont découvert le sacrement de réconciliation. L’eucharistie, l’adoration étaient au cœur de nos journées. Nourries en profondeur, elles étaient heureuses de vivre la fraternité à travers des échanges libres et en vérité .

Merci à chacune pour son implication avant ou pendant la retraite, et merci à Soeur Marie et père Damien pour leur présence tellement précieuse. Prions pour que les fruits de ce temps avec le seigneur se répandent dans les cœurs des pèlerines et au-delà !

blocks.html:
Marche des femmes 2024 

 

 

 

 

 

 

​Une fois pas an, nous organisons une marche pour toutes les femmes, pour nous ressourcer.  Cette année nous vous avons proposé un week-end entier à Point Reyes !

​

Accompagnées par les Pères Johannes et David, nous avons alternés entre topos, messes, réflexions, temps de partages, prières et randonnées. 

​

Plénitude, Harmonie, Bienveillance, Sérénité, Joie, Paix, Simplicité, Ferveur… Ces mots pourraient évoquer les arômes d’un grand cru de la Napa Valley, lentement mûri en fût de chêne. Mais ici, ils traduisent les fruits spirituels cueillis lors de la « Marche des Femmes » des 26 et 27 octobre derniers à Point Reyes. De fait, cette retraite a été comme une vinification pour notre communauté CathoSV, révélant de subtiles notes spirituelles qui ont encore resserré les liens entre ses membres et renforcé notre croissance dans la connaissance intérieure du Seigneur. En effet, vingt-deux femmes de notre communauté ont pris deux jours pour s’échapper du quotidien et se placer sous le regard bienveillant du Seigneur, autour du thème : « Tu as du prix à mes yeux et je t’aime ». Au programme : marche, prière, partage, relecture, chants, messe… de quoi faire le plein de l’Esprit Saint pour les mois à venir !

Quelques images bibliques ont touché au cœur de ce week-end. Le figuier, par exemple, symbole de la Parole de Dieu, nous a rappelé que Dieu, tel un jardinier patient, bêche joyeusement notre humus intérieur pour que nous portions toujours plus de fruits… Pas d’engrais chimiques, juste de la patience divine ! Puis, nous avons rencontré Zachée, alias « Monsieur Perché-sur-son-Sycomore », qui, malgré sa petite taille (haute comme trois pommes), a inspiré par sa générosité et son envie folle de suivre Jésus. Une belle leçon de vie… et de grimpe !
Le mot d’une participante résume bien ce qui s’est vécu : « Framily », un mélange de fraternité et de famille. En tout cas, la connexion a été si forte que nous nous sommes découverts sous notre vrai jour, sans filtre ni maquillage, dans une ambiance conviviale et pleine de confiance. Une petite flamme fraternelle s’est allumée, ravivant la lumière du Christ au milieu de nous.

Du côté des prêtres, nous avons eu la joie de former un duo mémorable. Tellement symbolique : un avant-goût de réconciliation entre clergé séculier et régulier, sans oublier la touche franco-allemande ! Le destin – ou plutôt le « clin Dieu » – a voulu que Père David soit l’ange gardien du Père Johannes pour le week-end (chacun des participants étant invité à prier spécialement pour un autre participant). Tout un programme !
Et que restera-t-il de cette retraite ? Quelques clichés inoubliables : le soleil couchant sur l’océan Pacifique, un verre à la main à l’heure de l’apéritif, mais surtout, une grande conviction que le Seigneur nous aime tels que nous sommes. Rendez-vous est donc déjà pris pour l’an prochain, histoire de revivre un peu de cette grâce qui nous a été donnée.

​

​

​

​

blocks.html:
Préparation des messes​

​

La messe est au cœur de notre vie de chrétiens et donc au cœur de notre mission de disciples du Christ. Préparer une messe, c'est participer à la vie de la communauté en se mettant au service de ses frères.

​

Merci à toutes celles et à toutes celles et ceux qui ont déjà participé à la préparation et l'animation des messes en français. 

 

​

​

​

​

Chaque messe est organisée par des volontaires de la communauté.

Les messes en français sont préparées par les membres de la communauté (familles, catéchistes, équipes Notre-Dame, groupe scout…), avec l'appui de l'équipe liturgie. 

 

Pourquoi organiser une messe?​

  • Cela fait partie de notre mission de chrétien.

  • Cela permet de mieux comprendre et donc de mieux aimer la messe. C'est l'occasion de vivre plus profondément la liturgie et de se mettre au service de la communauté.

  • C'est une expérience très riche, source de joie, qui fait beaucoup grandir dans la foi, en solo, en famille ou en groupe. 

  • C'est important. La communauté en a besoin, c'est le cœur de sa mission. S'il n'y a pas de volontaire pour préparer une messe, elle ne peut pas avoir lieu. 

  • Ce n'est pas difficile et cela s'adresse à tous. Quel que soit votre parcours de foi, vous avez beaucoup à apporter! L'équipe liturgie vous accompagne dans cette démarche. 

​

Comment organiser une messe?

Cela peut paraître impressionnant la première fois, mais pas de panique! L'équipe liturgie est là pour vous aider et a créé un kit de préparation.

​

Kit de préparation messe CathoSV.

​

En cas de question, l'équipe liturgie est toujours là, par email à liturgie@cathosv.org

​

Comment s'inscrire pour préparer?

C'est simple, cliquez dessous:

blocks.html: Comment est née CathoSV?
blocks.text: Comment est née CathoSV?

blocks.html: Un peu d’histoire pour commencer ! Les catholiques francophones de la région de San Francisco se regroupent dès leur arrivée en Californie, c’est-à-dire vers 1849 à l'époque de la Ruée vers l’Or. Les premières messes en français sont célébrées à la Mission Dolores (appelée à l'époque “San Francisco de Asis”). L’organisation de cette communauté s’adapte ensuite au gré des prêtres francophones sur place et des mouvements démographiques. Pendant plus de 200 ans, Notre-Dame-des-Victoires à San Francisco reste l'épicentre de la Communauté Catholique Francophone. Avec le départ en retraite du Père Siffert, les activités paroissiales en français ralentissent petit à petit, alors qu’au même moment la Silicon Valley connaît une croissance démographique. La population des ressortissants français, à titre d’exemple, est estimée aujourd’hui par le consulat à plus de 70,000 personnes et les établissements français ou bilingues se multiplient dans la région.

blocks.html: Plusieurs initiatives sont alors lancées dans la Baie et proposent des rassemblements oecuméniques, des groupes de prière ou la célébration de messes en français, le tout sans avoir de paroisse de rattachement ou de prêtre référent. C’est pour tenter de rassembler et de développer plus largement la Communauté Catholique Francophone qu’une start-up est créée! CathoSV dans sa forme actuelle, est née en 2017. C’est le nom choisi pour rassembler tous les Catholiques Francophones de la Silicon Valley, cette vaste région qui s'étend de Sonoma County à San Jose et de Oakland à San Francisco. Il existe aujourd’hui trois foyers principaux de CathoSV: South Bay (Los Altos), East Bay (Oakland) et San Francisco.

blocks.html: CathoSV, est-ce une association?
blocks.text: CathoSV, est-ce une association?

blocks.html: D’un point de vue statutaire, CathoSV est ce que l'on appelle ici "a parish based group", c'est à dire que nous sommes rattachés à une paroisse, en l'occurrence la paroisse St Nicholas & St William de Los Altos, choisie pour son point central et les liens de confiance tissés avec le curé et son équipe. Nous bénéficions ainsi des assurances, des infrastructures, des formations, du cadre juridique et financier de la paroisse mais aussi de toute la stabilité et des conseils de cette paroisse aux reins solides.

blocks.html: Quelle est la mission de CathoSV?
blocks.text: Quelle est la mission de CathoSV?

blocks.html: ​La mission de CathoSV est d’accueillir et de regrouper les Catholiques Francophones de la Baie de San Francisco pour leur permettre de vivre leur foi, la partager et la transmettre dans leur langue maternelle. Que l’on soit bilingue en anglais ou pas, pouvoir prier, chanter ou encore vivre des messes en français reste important pour la plupart d’entre nous. C’est aussi un moyen de soutenir la francophonie ! Ensuite, comme toute communauté catholique dans le monde, la mission principale de CathoSV est de faire de disciples de Jésus-Christ.
